title: Brian Mathews: Libraries spark the shared imagination our future needs | Editorial Columnists | dailyadvance.com
text:
Ten years ago, world leaders agreed on a set of priorities for the next generation. The idea was straightforward. If we want children and grandchildren to inherit a world with opportunity, stability and dignity, we have to make decisions today that move us in that direction.
These priorities include clean water, strong schools, reliable jobs, healthy communities, safe neighborhoods and a planet that can sustain future life. The United Nations called them Sustainable Development Goals, part of its 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and we now find ourselves entering the final stretch of that 15-year agenda.
Most people never directly engage with these global frameworks, yet the hopes behind them are familiar to anyone who cares about the future of their own town, county or region.
At their heart, these goals rest on a simple belief. Progress begins in the imagination. Every change starts as a picture in our minds, then in our conversations, and only later in our communities and institutions. This is not fanciful thinking. It is a practical skill, a kind of civic literacy, that allows us to see what could be better and take steady steps toward it.
In everyday life, imagination is often mistaken for wishful thinking. Yet throughout our shared civic experience, imagination is what has allowed communities to grow, solve challenges and reinvent themselves. Every school, hospital, public park and restored landscape began as a belief that things could be different. It took imagination to extend electricity into rural communities, to build highways that linked regions and to create community colleges and universities that opened doors for generations.
This raises an important question: Where do people actually develop this capacity? Where do they practice the literacy of imagination in daily life? One answer is surprisingly simple: libraries. They are among the few nonpartisan civic spaces where people learn, explore and encounter new ideas without pressure or polarization.
As a librarian, I’ve seen students, families and community members using these spaces to plan careers, solve problems and consider new opportunities. Libraries help people strengthen the very skill that the Sustainable Development Goals depend on: the ability to imagine what a better future might look like.
University libraries, in particular, bring together the diverse individuals found on college campuses in a single place to research, learn, discuss and collaborate. Here, students teach and challenge each other, unlocking the creative thinking and ambition required to reach their shared goals for the future.
By supporting both individual discovery and group engagement, university libraries are a place to remove division and push toward the same fundamental things most people want. A sense of belonging and safety. Homes and health care that families can afford. Good schools. Meaningful work.
The Sustainable Development Goals do not resolve division, but they offer scaffolding. They give us a shared horizon that does not belong to one political party. The Sustainable Development Goals remind us that most challenges require cooperation across many perspectives. Good jobs require both innovation and education. Healthy communities rely on reliable medical care and safe public spaces. Environmental stewardship connects farmers, business owners, scientists and families. No single group can carry these responsibilities alone.
We do not need to agree on every detail to move forward. We only need to begin facing the same direction. Shared imagination helps us see that our futures are connected. We rise together, we build together and we leave something meaningful behind together.
If we want to rekindle a sense of shared direction, we need to strengthen the civic capacity that makes progress possible. This is where imagination returns to the center. Civic imagination helps us picture a thriving downtown, safer sidewalks, welcoming public spaces, better jobs and a healthier environment for the generations that follow. Without imagination, we risk accepting decline as inevitable. With it, we create momentum and possibility.
I see collective imagination as a serious civic act. It sparks the ideas that become action. It turns a community’s aspirations into achievable steps. This is the work that libraries help sustain. They give people the tools to understand the present and the space to picture the future. In that sense, they function as imagination infrastructure for their communities, helping people strengthen the civic capacity that progress depends on.
There is another lesson in this 10-year milestone. Progress usually comes from steady, unglamorous work. Big speeches have their place, but real change happens in city halls, classrooms, health clinics, small businesses, neighborhood groups and, yes, libraries. It happens when volunteers show up, when parents invest in their children and when citizens choose patience over cynicism. This quiet work does not trend online, yet it shapes the future far more than the arguments on our screens.
The Sustainable Development Goals are not perfect. No plan this large ever is. But they remind us that progress begins with a shared sense of what is possible. If we dare to imagine a better future and choose cooperation over competition, we give ourselves a real chance to shape it. The work ahead will not be easy, but it will be stronger when we meet it with tolerance, hope and a willingness to work side by side.
